sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element (primary buttons, links, cards, section headings, error states) look the same everywhere it appears?** No. The four "Add to cart" buttons (y≈542–588, one per card at x≈65, 367, 668, 970) do the same job but come in four colours: teal, purple, amber-orange and blue. A shopper will read the colours as meaning something, such as a different action, a sale, or a category, and can't find out what. The row also turns into a rainbow strip that pulls the eye away from the plants and prices, and it breaks the calm green and terracotta mood the rest of the page sets. The same role should get the same colour everywhere (Material Design 3, Color roles; Apple HIG, Color; Nielsen heuristic 4, Consistency and standards; Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*, on repeated elements following one program). Fix: give all four buttons one shared primary colour, ideally one taken from the page's own palette, such as a deep green. Keep a different colour only for a real difference in role or state. Defect / convention. Weight: major. It is the one thing that makes this otherwise tidy page look unconsidered, and it implies a difference between the products that doesn't exist.

**What's working.**
- The page's job is clear in one glance. "Low-light houseplants" plus the subhead "Four plants that do well more than six feet from a window" tells you what the page is, who it's for, and gives a concrete reference point (six feet) instead of a vague claim. The copy is finished and specific.
- Apart from the buttons, the palette fits the message: muted sage picture tiles, leaf green, terracotta pots and lots of white. It feels calm and domestic, which suits a houseplant shop.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each kind of element looks the same everywhere: four "Add to cart" buttons in four different colours)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. The title "Low-light houseplants" (about 48–375 × 92–125) is the largest type on the page, but it is plain dark text. The four "Add to cart" buttons across y≈542–588 are solid, saturated blocks, and each is a different hue: teal, purple, orange and blue. They are the strongest contrast on the page. On first look the eye goes to the orange and purple buttons, moves between all four, and only then reaches the title. The buttons are all the same size and weight, and none is stronger than the others, so instead of one starting point there are four places competing to be first. Tschichold's *The New Typography* says the order of importance should be plain, with one element seen first. The fix is to make the title, or the product row as a whole, the clear starting point, and pull the buttons back to one shared, calmer treatment. One button colour, used the same way on every card, keeps them visible as actions without letting them lead the page. The colour section may raise the same buttons as a palette problem; here the point is only that they take the eye from the title. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. In each card, the product name (e.g. "Snake plant", 65,450) and the price ("$24", 65,512) are both bold and near-black, and they look about 18 px and 20 px. That is almost the same size, with the price a touch larger. So neither reads as the card's heading, and the price looks like a near-copy of the name instead of its own level. The logo "Fernhill Plants" (48,28) also looks the same size and weight as the product names. Dair (*Design with Type*, ch. 8) says weak contrast is worse than none: a difference of one size step looks like an accident. The fix is to give the name and the price an obvious difference in size, weight or colour, and to decide which one leads the card. For a shopper comparing plants, that is usually the name, with the price set clearly apart. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** Headings and body text differ by more than size. The title and product names are bold near-black, while the subtitle and spec lines ("6 in pot, grows to 2 ft") are regular weight and mid-grey. Inside each card, the descriptive detail clearly sits below the name. Keep that weight-and-colour split when the name and price sizes are adjusted.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element stands clearly above the rest; each text level distinct, no two sizes almost the same).

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None. I answered all 13 lines yes.

The four "Add to cart" buttons are the same action in four hues (teal, purple, orange, blue, at y≈542–588). That doesn't fail this section's similarity line, because it puts no unrelated things into a group. It does stop the row from reading as one repeated set, and it belongs to the colour section ("Limited, purposeful palette"). I'm passing it to the director so it isn't lost.

**What's working.**
- **One strict grid.** The page has four equal columns, each card about 280 px wide, with even gutters of about 22 px. A 48 px left edge is shared by the logo, the title, the subtitle and the first card, and a 1232 px right edge is shared by "Cart (0)" and the last card. The header, the heading and the product row all hang off the same two lines, so the page reads as one ordered piece (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*).
- **Card contents line up across the row.** Image tiles, names (y≈450), specs (y≈478), prices (y≈512) and buttons all sit at the same heights in every card. A shopper can compare sizes and prices by reading straight across, which is what a four-plant comparison is for.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (Text)**: body size yes; caption size yes (the gray spec lines look about 13 px but are crisp); plain face yes; one family (Inter-like) yes; weights yes; contrast yes (the gray subtitle and spec lines look about #4b5563 on white, well above 4.5:1); text over image n/a yes; line length n/a yes (no paragraphs); leading n/a yes; multi-line heading n/a yes; flush left yes; justified n/a yes; rag n/a yes; widows yes; breaks yes; paragraph marks n/a yes; left edges yes; chunking yes; mixed case yes; emphasis yes; display spacing yes; kerning yes; tracking yes; caps n/a yes; ligatures n/a yes (the headline has no fi or fl); real cuts yes; quotes and dashes yes (the hyphen in "Low-light" is correct); tabular figures n/a yes; real type yes; nothing clipped yes. No line is no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The type scale is tight and every size has a job. There are about four levels: the page title at about 30 px bold, the product name and price at about 18–20 px semibold or bold, the nav and subtitle at about 14–15 px, and the spec lines at about 13 px in gray. The levels are told apart by weight and gray value rather than by sizes only a little apart, so the price stands out in each card without a fifth size.
- The copy reads cleanly for a stranger. "Four plants that do well more than six feet from a window" gives the viewer a concrete test of their own room instead of a vague "low light". Each spec line ("6 in pot, grows to 2 ft") gives a number, a unit and a point of reference, so the buyer knows the pot size and the mature size before adding to cart.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I reviewed the Color section of this 1280×800 plant-shop page by eye. Bash was blocked, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. The image is one screen, so the whole image was enough, and I read the colour references directly.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece use a small palette, about one neutral range and one or two hues besides the status colors?** No. The four "Add to cart" buttons (y≈542–588, at x≈65–311, 367–612, 668–914 and 970–1215) are four different strong hues: teal, purple, burnt orange and blue. Apart from these, the page is all neutrals plus the leaf green and terracotta of the illustrations, so the buttons are the only strong colour on the page.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** four buttons that do the same job look like four different actions. Shoppers may look for a meaning, such as a category, a care level or a sale, and there isn't one. The row looks like a rainbow placeholder, not a shop with its own colour, and no brand colour comes through.
   - **Why:** Refactoring UI, "Define your shades", and Material Design 3 colour roles say a piece should have a small defined palette, with one colour per role. Material 3 and Apple HIG Color say the same role uses the same colour everywhere. Itten (colour chords) says that several vivid hues at equal weight give the eye no lead colour.
   - **Fix:** give all four buttons one shared colour and make that the brand's single accent. A deep green that matches the leaves would tie it to the plants. Keep a different colour only for a different role or state.
   - **Type and weight:** defect (it can suggest a meaning that isn't there) and convention. Major.
2. **Do warm colors sit on what should come forward and cool ones on what should recede?** No. The burnt-orange button under "Cast iron plant" (x≈668–914, y≈542–588) is the only warm, high-chroma shape in the row. It comes forward more than the teal, purple and blue buttons, and its hue is close to the terracotta pots, so it pulls the eye to the third card for no reason. Nothing marks that plant as featured.
   - **Why:** Itten, warm–cool contrast. Warm colours advance, so they belong on the focal element.
   - **Fix:** this goes away with the fix to Finding 1. If one product really should be promoted, mark it on purpose with a label and not just with button temperature.
   - **Type and weight:** convention. Minor. It is a side effect of Finding 1.

**What's working.**
- **Neutral base:** the page is almost all neutral (white ground, pale grey-green image panels, near-black and grey text). So the little colour there is has room to work, and the structure holds up in grayscale: dark headings and prices, white cards, dark buttons with white labels.
- **Illustrations:** the same green leaf and terracotta pot repeat across all four cards. That gives the page a consistent, calm plant identity, and the fixed button colour could pick it up.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 7 yes, 2 no (small palette; warm forward, cool back), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes to the "Low-light houseplants" heading, then across four matching cards. Each card has a pale green tile with a flat cartoon plant in a terracotta pot, and then the four different coloured buttons pull the eye down. It reads as a small, tidy, generic shop page. The 1280×800 image fits on one screen, so no crops are needed. Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole image.

The job, assumed: a product listing page where shoppers pick a low-light houseplant and add it to their cart.

Pictures:
- Every image shows its content: **no**. The four tiles (65–311, 367–612, 668–914, 970–1215 × 193–423) are the same generic plant drawing with the leaves rearranged. None of them shows the actual plant. Common sense, no catalog entry.
- Full quality: yes
- Crops look intended: yes. The pot sits about 8 px above the bottom of the tile, which reads as standing on a floor.
- Figure-ground: yes
- One rendering style and level of detail: yes
- Photos treated consistently: yes (there are no photos)
- Icons share stroke, cap, and corners: yes (there are no icons)
- One viewpoint and light: yes
- Quiet texture: yes
- No fake depth: yes
- Logo with clear space: yes. The "Fernhill Plants" wordmark at 48,28 has plenty of room.
- Mark simple enough: yes

The only `no` line has no catalog entry, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There are four product illustrations and a text wordmark.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No. The four product tiles in the upper half of each card (for example x 65–311, y 193–423) are not photos or faithful drawings of the plants for sale. They are one template: the same terracotta pot, the same green, and two or three almond-shaped leaves in different arrangements.
   - **What the shopper meets:** the tiles look like they show the product, so the shopper takes them as what will arrive, and they mislead.
   - The snake plant should be tall, stiff, upright blades, not one broad leaf and a stub.
   - The ZZ plant should be stems of small glossy leaflets, not two broad leaves.
   - The pothos card says "trails to 6 ft", but the drawing is two upright leaves with nothing trailing.
   - The cast iron plant is listed with an 8 in pot, but its pot is drawn the same size as the 6 in pots.
   - A shopper choosing between four plants by look gets almost nothing from the pictures. They have to rely on the names and already know what each plant looks like. On a shop page the product picture is usually what sells the item, so the page gives up its main reason to buy.
   - **Why:** common sense (no catalog entry). On a product listing the picture is the product's evidence.
   - **Direction of the fix:** use real photos of each plant in the pot that is sold, shot and cropped the same way. If it has to stay illustrated, draw each plant's real shape (blades, leaflets, trailing vines) and scale the pots to the sizes listed.
   - If these are placeholders waiting for photos, the finding is that they ship looking finished.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.

**What's working.** The four tiles are well matched with each other. They use the same flat style, level of detail, palette, front-on view, and pale green ground, and each plant is placed in its tile the same way. So the row reads as one calm set. The plants also stand out clearly against the pale tile. Keep that consistency when the pictures are replaced.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a top navigation, a cart link and four "Add to cart" buttons.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?** The four "Add to cart" buttons, about 246×46 px each at y≈542–588 (x≈65, 367, 668, 970), are filled in four different colours: teal, purple, orange and blue. Repeating one filled button per product card is the normal shop pattern, so the problem is not the number of buttons. The problem is that each one has its own colour. People read a change of colour as a change of meaning, so the shopper is left wondering whether the purple button does something the teal one doesn't, or whether the orange one is a sale. On top of that, four saturated colours side by side are the loudest thing on the page. Where the cards meet the eye, it lands on the button row before the plants, the names or the prices. Material Design 3 ("Buttons") says to give the most important action one high-emphasis style, and here that style is split four ways, so no colour ever comes to mean "buy". Fix: give every "Add to cart" button the same single brand colour, so the colour means "this adds to your cart" wherever it appears, and let the plant illustrations be the part that changes from card to card. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step, progress, or loading?** The top-right navigation (y≈28: "Houseplants", "Pots", "Care guides", "Cart (0)") draws every item the same. This page is a houseplant category, but "Houseplants" isn't marked as the current section, and there is no breadcrumb linking "Low-light houseplants" back to its parent. The heading tells the visitor what page this is but not where it sits in the shop, so someone who arrived from search can't tell that this is one subset of Houseplants. Laubheimer, "Menu-Design Checklist" (Nielsen Norman Group), guideline 5, says to indicate the user's current location in the menu. Fix: mark "Houseplants" with one clear cue, such as a bolder weight, an underline or a bar, and consider a one-line breadcrumb above the heading. Convention. Weight: minor, because the page heading already names the page.

**What's working.** "Cart (0)" sits top right with its count showing. That is exactly where shoppers look for it (Jakob's law, Nielsen), and the shopper can see the cart's state before adding anything. Each card also puts its "Add to cart" button directly under the price and the plant it buys, so every button clearly belongs to its own item (Norman, natural mapping).

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the buttons and nav links show a visible focus ring of at least 2 px at 3:1 contrast, and whether pressing "Add to cart" gives visible feedback, such as the cart count changing to (1) or a confirmation. On a shop page that feedback is the only sign the click worked, so check it in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 2 no (one primary action style; shows where the user is), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
